https://www.dw.com/en/guatemala-towns-ev.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IFPg Fuego volcano erupted twice last year as well Image: AFP Advertisement Guatemala's disaster management agency CONRED issued evacuation notices for several towns near the highly active Volcan de Fuego on Tuesday, as it spewed columns of lava, gas, and ash some four kilometers (2.5 miles) into the sky. The volcano is located some 40 kilometers (25 miles) southwest of Guatemala City. CONRED issued an orange warning, its second-highest level, and urged residents to move to emergency shelters outside of the volcano's path. Schools have been closed in the area and some businesses have temporarily shuttered. According to the agency, ash clouds have traveled as far as 60 kilometers (37 miles) to the west of the volcano, and could significantly disrupt air traffic in the area. Guatemala's Institute of Seismology and Volcanology stressed that the volcano is experiencing its "most intense phase" and that people should be extremely careful with a 10-kilometer (6.2-mile) radius of it. Hikers warned to leave area Local media reported that onlookers continued to climb the nearby Acatenango volcano, despite a safety ban, in order to take videos of the eruption to post on social media. Volcan de Fuego is nearly 3,800 meters (12,500 feet) tall and sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire . It is one of the most active volcanoes in Central America, and in 2018 a violent eruption claimed the lives of some 200 people. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg4d.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, (From left): Swans players Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and James Jordon have been suspended. By Harry Sekulich Reporting from Sydney Published 3 hours ago Five players in the Australian Football League (AFL) have been banned for late-night drinking and inviting women to a hotel after a weekend match in Melbourne. The Sydney Swans' Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice have been stood down from Australian Rules football's top league for the rest of the season, the club announced. The suspension comes after detectives in Melbourne began an investigation into an alleged sexual assault, said to have to taken place in the early hours of Monday morning at the Pullman Hotel where the players were staying after the match. None of the players have been arrested or charged in the investigation. Sydney Swans chairman Andrew Pridham apologised to fans, players and the wider community on Wednesday. Speaking to reporters, he explained that the sanctions were handed down because the players had breached the club's standards by drinking alcohol later than accepted and bringing women to the hotel. In a statement published earlier in the day announcing the suspensions, the club said: "We respect there is an ongoing investigation by Victoria Police and the actions we have taken today are independent of this. "The AFL is supportive of the Club's sanctions." Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich told a media conference: "We're deeply embarrassed and ashamed that the poor choices of five of our players, and the impact that's had on the women involved and also the club. "We are deeply concerned about their welfare and the wellbeing of those women." He declined to say whether any of the players had been drug tested, saying that any testing would form part of the police inquiry. A spokesperson for Victoria Police said officers have spoken to several people who were at the Pullman Hotel, but no one was formally interviewed or arrested. On Tuesday, club officials held talks with the players ahead of their suspension. AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon has described the reports of the alleged sexual assault as "deeply concerning". Sydney has dominated this season, currently placing second on the ladder which guarantees them a spot in the qualifying and elimination finals' round that begins in two weeks. The club is scheduled to play against North Melbourne at the Sydney Cricket Ground on Sunday, which will be the last fixture ahead of the finals. Heeney and Warner are considered two of the sport's biggest stars. Unlike some other Australian sports, the AFL does not have a strict no-fault stand-down policy on players charged with serious offences such as sexual assault, and instead handles cases on a discretionary and case-by-case basis. https://baltic-review.com/rezekne-latvia.text: Share Tweet 0 Rēzekne will host the KOPUMS Youth Opportunities Festival on 12 August 2026. Rēzekne is preparing to host Latvia’s Youth Opportunities Festival “KOPUMS” on Wednesday, 12 August 2026, bringing young people, youth workers, public institutions and non-governmental organisations together for a day focused on practical opportunities and participation. The event is part of Rēzekne’s year as Latvia’s Youth Capital and is scheduled to begin at 13:00. ([researchlatvia.gov.lv](https://www.researchlatvia.gov.lv/lv/events/jauniesu-iespeju-festivals-kopums?utm_source=openai)) The festival is designed as an open meeting point rather than a single-stage cultural event. According to the Rēzekne tourism centre’s programme, more than 60 organisations from across Latvia are expected to take part in an information and activity area at the city’s Olympic Centre. Visitors will be able to learn about youth initiatives, education, employment, volunteering and other forms of involvement while taking part in workshops, competitions and creative activities. ([visit.rezekne.lv](https://visit.rezekne.lv/event/jauniesu-iespeju-festivals-kopums/?utm_source=openai)) A nationwide meeting in Latgale Rēzekne’s selection as Latvia’s Youth Capital gives the festival a broader role in the country’s youth policy calendar. The city has been presenting itself throughout 2026 as a place for youth development, community involvement and exchange between young people and organisations working with them. The “KOPUMS” programme is intended to make those connections visible in a public, informal setting. The Ministry of Welfare’s National Employment Agency, or NVA, is among the institutions taking part. Its specialists plan to provide information about career planning, skills sought by employers, labour-market opportunities and available support services. The agency also says that young visitors will be able to complete professional suitability tests and discuss questions about their next education or employment steps with advisers. ([nva.gov.lv](https://www.nva.gov.lv/lv/notikums/nva-piedalisies-jauniesu-iespeju-festivala-kopums-rezekne?utm_source=openai)) That practical emphasis is one of the festival’s most useful features. For young people from smaller towns and rural areas, a single day bringing together employment advisers, education-related organisations, civic groups and creative initiatives can offer a concentrated introduction to options that may otherwise be scattered across different websites and institutions. This is an editorial inference based on the published participant list and programme, rather than a claim about measured outcomes. Workshops, movement and the city The programme combines information with activities intended to make participation social and accessible. At the ARPC “Zeimuļs” creative centre, visitors can join guided tours of the distinctive green-roofed building, with tours planned at 14:00, 15:00 and 16:00. The same venue is scheduled to host the “Freestyle Summer 2026” breakdance competition from 13:30 to 17:00. ([visit.rezekne.lv](https://visit.rezekne.lv/event/jauniesu-iespeju-festivals-kopums/?utm_source=openai)) At the Olympic Centre, a large dance concert is planned for 16:30. The published programme says that more than 300 dancers from Rēzekne will perform. The evening programme is due to continue with a concert by the Latgalian hip-hop group “Latgalīšu Reps” at 20:00. ([visit.rezekne.lv](https://visit.rezekne.lv/event/jauniesu-iespeju-festivals-kopums/?utm_source=openai)) Outdoor activities will also connect the festival with the city’s public spaces. Organisers have announced canoe trips along the Rēzekne River promenade, running from the city sign towards “Zeimuļs”, with departures listed for 14:00 and 15:30. Participation requires advance registration because places are limited. ([visit.rezekne.lv](https://visit.rezekne.lv/event/jauniesu-iespeju-festivals-kopums/?utm_source=openai)) Part of a continuing youth programme “KOPUMS” is linked to International Youth Day, observed on 12 August, and is intended not only for young people looking for new opportunities but also for youth workers seeking professional exchange and new contacts. Earlier announcements invited organisations, municipalities and state institutions to contribute activities, discussions and workshops. The organisers also said the festival would be used to announce the next Latvian Youth Capital for 2027. ([jaunatneslietas.gov.lv](https://jaunatneslietas.gov.lv/current-events/organizacijas-un-valsts-parvalde-aicinatas-pieteik-aktivitates-jauniesu-iespeju?utm_source=openai)) Rēzekne’s municipal information archive has separately reported preparations involving volunteers from several Latvian municipalities, including Mārupe, Kārsava, Valmiera, Preiļi and Riga. That cross-regional preparation underlines the event’s national rather than purely local character. ([rezekne.lv](https://rezekne.lv/visas-zinas/?utm_source=openai)) For Rēzekne, the festival offers a constructive way to use the Youth Capital title: not simply as a year-long label, but as a platform where young people can compare experiences, discover services and meet organisations in person. For visitors, “KOPUMS” presents a full day of civic, educational and cultural activity in the centre of Latgale. https://business-review.eu/business/lega.text: Filip & Company secures in favour of ROMATSA the annulment of a decision that could have disrupted Romanian air traffic Filip & Company law firm announces a significant victory before the High Court of Cassation and Justice (ICCJ). Having taken on the case in the final appeal, the firm’s team succeeded in overturning the decision of the Bucharest Court of Appeal, which had ordered a 30-day suspension of ROMATSA’s operating licence. ROMATSA’s appeal was upheld, and the decision is final. The stakes in this case were unprecedented: the suspension of ROMATSA’s operating licence would have resulted in the closure of Romania’s airspace, with potentially catastrophic consequences for both military and civilian operations. This would have effectively halted all commercial and military flights to and from Romania, with a direct impact on national security and on the millions of passengers transiting Romanian airspace. “ It was a case with implications that were quite unique, because the effects of a court ruling went far beyond the legal relationship between the parties involved. The suspension of ROMATSA’s operating licence would have had direct consequences for the functioning of air traffic in Romania, so it was essential to construct a very rigorous legal argument in the final appeal and, at the same time, to put the specific implications of the case into context. We are grateful that the High Court upheld the appeal and that our contribution helped secure a final ruling in such an important case ”, said Adrian Cristea, Senior Associate at Filip & Company . Essentially, the dispute centred on ROMATSA’s decision to use the FEAST test conducted via the Eurocontrol platform, rather than directly recruiting individuals who held a trainee air traffic controller’s licence obtained from a civil aviation school. The Bucharest Court of Appeal had ruled that this practice constituted repeated acts of discrimination and had ordered the suspension of the operating licence. Read more about Filip & Company assists a syndicate of five banks in arranging a EUR 187 million sustainability-linked loan for MOOV Leasing read more At the hearing of the final appeal, the Filip & Company team was successful in having all procedural objections raised by the opposing party dismissed directly during the court session, which was subsequently followed by the pleadings on the merits of the appeal. The Filip & Company team that assisted ROMATSA on this case consisted of Adrian Cristea (senior associate) and Bogdan Fărcane (associate). This victory was also made possible by George Trantea (partner) and Cristina Tudoran (partner) who contributed valuable ideas that helped shape our legal arguments. With the final appeal upheld, Romania’s airspace remains fully operational, and ROMATSA can seamlessly continue its essential air traffic management activities. https://www.koreaherald.com/article/1087.text: Estonian defense firms pitch battlefield know-how, NATO access to Korean partners Published : Sept. 17, 2026 - 12:00:44 Updated : Sept. 17, 2026 - 17:55:24 Add The Korea Herald on Google Link copied! Hwang Joo-young Staff reporter at The Korea Herald’s National Desk, based in Seoul. Covers South Korea’s national security and foreign policy, with a focus on the Defense, Foreign and Unification Ministries, as well as the National Assembly. Before entering journalism, served as an Air Force officer. Experience includes providing translation and interpretation, as well as strategic input for planning efforts, at the ROK-US Combined Forces Command. During three years of military service, took part in six major South Korea-US combined exercises. Subscribe + Marko Kaseleht, founder of Estonian battlefield intelligence company SensusQ and senior vice president for defense at Nortal, speaks with South Korean reporters at the EIS headquarters in Tallinn on Wednesday. (Joint Press Corps) Korea Herald correspondent TALLINN, Estonia — For Estonian defense companies seeking deeper ties with South Korea, one of their selling points is something money alone cannot easily buy: experience. “The lessons learned, lessons identified from Ukraine, it is something that is measured in gold right now,” said Marko Kaseleht, founder of Estonian battlefield intelligence company SensusQ. “Getting feedback, understanding how your adversaries are collaborating, all that is something that everybody is after,” he told South Korean reporters Wednesday at the headquarters of Enterprise Estonia, or EIS, in Tallinn. Kaseleht, who spent 15 years in the Estonian military before entering the defense industry, also serves as senior vice president for defense at Nortal, an Estonian software and digital transformation company. Since Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Estonia, which shares a border with Russia, has developed close defense ties with Kyiv. Estonian companies have supplied technologies to Ukraine and used feedback from the battlefield to update their products as threats and tactics evolve. Kaseleht said some of the most valuable lessons involve unmanned systems. “I think the most important knowledge that they currently have is everything related with unmanned aerial and unmanned ground systems. Not only the offensive but the defensive part as well,” he said. Significance for Seoul That experience carries particular relevance for South Korea as North Korean troops and weapons have become involved in Russia’s war. South Korean military and intelligence authorities estimate that North Korea has deployed roughly 14,000 to 15,000 troops to Russia's campaign since late 2024. According to reports, North Korean troops adapted their tactics after initially suffering losses to Ukrainian first-person-view drones; a captured North Korean soldier said his unit had used Russian anti-drone jamming equipment. Kaseleht argued that the transfer of wartime knowledge could pose a concern for Seoul. “Everything that Russia is doing potentially will land on North Korea’s knowledge base,” he said, referring to lessons from hybrid warfare and other battlefield scenarios. Marduk Technologies, an Estonian counter-drone company, is exploring how such knowledge-sharing could work with South Korean partners. Rauno Lember, the company’s chief operating officer, said Marduk continually updates the software behind its drone-detection systems to recognize new Russian, Chinese and North Korean models appearing over Ukraine. “If the cooperation fully gets underway, the sharing of knowledge and data will naturally take place,” Lember said of potential cooperation with South Korean companies. “That’s our business logic,” he said. Still, such sharing is not entirely up to the companies themselves. Rene Ehasalu, cluster manager at the Estonian Defence and Aerospace Industry Association, pointed to European Union rules on technology transfers and sensitive information, as well as Estonia’s export licensing process. Nonetheless, he said battlefield experience accumulated by Estonian companies in Ukraine could be shared if joint research, development or capability-building projects with Korean companies materialize. “Honestly, there has so far been no precedent in which the government directly intervened or put the brakes on technology or information sharing between private companies,” Ehasalu said. North Korean soldiers participate in a demonstration during training by the Korean People’s Army’s air and amphibious combat units, in this photo released in March 2024. (KCNA via Yonhap) Estonia’s defense buildup Estonia’s increasingly proactive approach toward South Korea comes as it ramps up defense spending and expands its defense industry. Estonia is spending 2.4 billion euros ($2.75 billion) on defense this year, equivalent to 5.4 percent of gross domestic product and up 42 percent from 2025. More than half of the budget is earmarked for procurement, while Tallinn plans to keep defense spending above 5 percent of GDP in the coming years. The country’s defense industry recorded turnover of 730 million euros in 2025, including 450 million euros in exports, and is targeting 2 billion euros by 2030. For Estonian companies, South Korea offers something Europe increasingly lacks: the ability to manufacture weapons at scale and deliver them quickly. Kaseleht said European defense manufacturers are struggling with production bottlenecks as orders pile up years in advance. “The Korean defense industry, and overall industry, is extremely strong at platforms, production and scale,” he said, also highlighting South Korea’s ability to deliver systems quickly. Hanwha Aerospace has been the most visible example of that defense relationship. The company has exported K9 self-propelled howitzers to Estonia, while Tallinn has also contracted for nine Chunmoo multiple rocket launchers. The first six were ordered in late 2025, with three additional systems ordered in May. Kaseleht said such cooperation should go beyond individual arms sales. “Let’s not look at this as a supplier-customer relationship,” he said. “It’s much more.” Hanwha signed a memorandum of understanding with Nortal and SensusQ in September 2025 to jointly develop a next-generation battlefield management system, including for platforms such as the Redback. It has also signed a separate agreement with Marduk on counter-drone cooperation. Other Korean defense companies are pursuing opportunities in Estonia as well. HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and Hanwha Ocean, part of Hanwha Group, are among four companies competing for Estonia’s planned acquisition of new naval vessels, alongside Sweden’s Saab and Estonia’s Baltic Workboats. NATO gateway Another potential benefit is access to the broader European and NATO ecosystem by adapting Korean systems to European and NATO standards. Kaseleht said the two countries’ strengths could complement each other in that process, with South Korea strong in weapons platforms, manufacturing scale and delivery, and Estonia specializing in software, data and cybersecurity. “So if we put Korean platforms together with NATO-interoperable software layers that are built in Estonia, we actually get products that are ready for EU and NATO markets,” he said. “It’s much more. It’s an opportunity for both countries to develop something that doesn’t exist worldwide.” When asked whether integrating Korean defense systems with Estonian technology could help them fit into the wider NATO ecosystem, Rannar Park, head of business engagement at the e-Estonia Briefing Centre under EIS, said shared NATO standards could make interoperability more important than the origin of individual technologies. “It doesn't matter if the technology is Estonian, Korean or somewhere in between,” Park said. “Rather, it's NATO technology. It's defense technology that can benefit all sides.” The concept is not entirely theoretical. Estonia has already modified communications and control equipment on its K9 howitzers to fit its operational environment, and a similar process is expected as the country introduces Chunmoos. South Korea is also moving in the same direction. In August, the Defense Acquisition Program Administration, the country’s state arms procurement agency, introduced its first formal guidelines allowing Korean defense companies to obtain NATO standards, aimed at improving interoperability and helping them compete in NATO markets. Russia factor There is, however, a geopolitical limit to how closely Seoul can embrace the Estonian proposition. For Estonia, Russia is the immediate military threat and support for Ukraine is closely tied to its own national security. For South Korea, the calculation is more complicated. A Seoul official, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the issue, said South Korea could not simply disregard its relationship with Moscow, which remains a factor in security on the Korean Peninsula, including the North Korean nuclear issue. The official said Korean companies should first show that they understand Estonia’s security concerns before focusing on arms sales. Kaseleht meanwhile sees the calculation differently. He argued that Russia’s expanding military cooperation with North Korea has already changed the strategic environment facing South Korea. “South Korea shouldn’t be afraid to establish a better and stronger dialogue, both political and business, with Ukrainians,” Kaseleht said. “That is only going to help you.” He added that closer engagement with Ukraine would not necessarily have to mean supplying lethal weapons, pointing to medicine, protective equipment and generators as other possible forms of support. Asked whether additional formal arrangements were needed to deepen cooperation, Kaseleht said existing mechanisms were sufficient. “The framework exists,” he said. “What we’re lacking, we’re lacking actual projects, actual programs.” Wednesday’s session was arranged by Enterprise Estonia for South Korean reporters visiting Tallinn as part of the Korea Press Foundation’s “2026 KPF Diploma Program: Security in the AI Era.” Rauno Lember, chief operating officer of Estonian counter-drone company Marduk Technologies, speaks with South Korean reporters at the EIS headquarters in Tallinn on Wednesday. Photograph: Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Alastair Campbell, co-host of popular podcast The Rest is Politics and former staffer for UK prime minister Tony Blair, said the tenor of political debate in Australia should better reflect Helen Haines’ own approach. Photograph: Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto/Getty Images Australian politics Australia must ‘re-win the argument for democratic politics’ in wake of Haines incident, Alastair Campbell says Tony Blair’s former spokesperson says attacks on UK MPs did not bring about lasting cultural change and overheated rhetoric quickly returned to politics Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Tom McIlroy Political editor Wed 28 Oct 2026 02.24 EDT Last modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 02.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Tony Blair’s former communications guru, Alastair Campbell , says the UK political system was too quick to revert to overheated rhetoric and polarisation after attacks on MPs, urging politicians to “re-win the argument for democratic politics”. More than a week after independent MP Helen Haines was allegedly targeted in an attack outside her electorate office in northern Victoria, causing her to lose both legs, Campbell said the tenor of political debate in Australia should better reflect Haines’ own approach. Alastair Campbell on Trump, political violence and why populist politics doesn’t work - podcast Read more Speaking to the Guardian’s Australian Politics podcast on Wednesday, the commentator said the killings of British MPs Jo Cox, David Amess and former politician Ann Widdecombe had not brought about lasting change in political culture. “They were followed by everybody saying the right thing about how our political debate culture had to change, about how we had to address online hate and polarisation, all this stuff,” he said. “But it didn’t take long before we kind of got right back into it. So I think it is about how we genuinely try and generate a different way of talking to each other and about each other now.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email A 43-year-old man has been charged over the alleged attack on Haines and the incident continues to be investigated by police. The co-host of popular podcast The Rest is Politics, Campbell said Haines’ eventual return to parliament would help bring about change. “It’s very rare these days that an individual act or incident lasts more than half a news cycle, and so we just move on. I think remembering is so important. “In a way, the fact that she is still with us and is going to still be part of the political debate, maybe that will help people … that people will see that that is the consequence of the actions that were taken against her.” A former journalist, Campbell is the author of more than 20 books, including diaries documenting his years working inside 10 Downing Street. He is due to visit Australia for a speaking tour next month. Campbell said politicians and the media should reflect on how they speak to everyday people, and why their professions are so poorly trusted. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “It’s made more difficult at the moment because you’ve got Donald Trump in America as the loudest, most talked about politician on the planet, and he represents a lot of the things that I think we don’t want in our politics. “We’ve got to re-win the argument for democratic politics because it’s under a lot of pressure right now,” he said. Discussing the rise of populist politics, Campbell said the world was still struggling to grasp the effects of the 2008 global financial crisis. “If I think of one thing that maybe ties the rise of Trump to Brexit, to the protests that we’re seeing in different parts of Europe, I think is that we haven’t really come to terms with the consequences of the financial crisis, and the sense that there was socialism for the banks who caused it, and austerity for the people, and the people who are still struggling to see their living standards rise. “That, ultimately I think, is a big driver of what the Americans call affordability, what we call cost of living, just the sense that people don’t feel that they’re able to get on.” Campbell revealed he occasionally watches clips of Paul Keating’s parliamentary attacks as Australia’s prime minister in the 1990s. The bestselling author’s latest book is Persevilience: The Word the World Needs Now, published by Allen and Unwin.
